A 83-year-old male presents to the emergency department with complaints of abdominal pain, nausea,
and vomiting. He reports diffuse abdominal tenderness. His medical history includes diabetic
nephropathy, hypertension, dyslipidemia, depression, and morbid obesity. He is also undergoing
treatment for a genital herpes outbreak. His vital signs are as follows: temperature 97.7°F (37.2°C),
blood pressure 191/109 mmHg, pulse 63/min, respirations 12/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room
air. On physical examination, he is noted to be obese but in no acute distress. A CT scan of the
abdomen with contrast reveals no abnormalities. The patient is admitted for observation, and his
abdominal pain improves following an enema and multiple bowel movements. Evening lab results are
as follows: Serum: Na+: 141 mEq/L Cl-: 99 mEq/L K+: 4.8 mEq/L HCO3-: 11 mEq/L BUN: 65 mg/dL
Glucose: 177 mg/dL Creatinine: 3.1 mg/dL (baseline: 2.8 mg/dL) Which of the following is the most
likely cause of this patient’s laboratory abnormalities? Answer Choices: (A) Hypovolemia-induced
prerenal azotemia (B) Dehydration from poor oral intake (C) Diabetic ketoacidosis (D) Non-anion gap
metabolic acidosis from diarrhea (E) Atorvastatin (F) Hyperkalemia-induced metabolic acidosis (G)
Metformin (H) Acute tubular necrosis from contrast nephropathy (I) Lactic acidosis from bowel ischemia
(J) Acyclovir
